metaDescription: Five 5G-compatible cell phone signal boosters compared by gain, coverage and carrier bands, with an honest look at what 5G support really means.
introParagraphs: Almost every booster now says 5G on the box, which makes the label nearly meaningless on its own. The five kits here all list 5G compatibility, and they differ in the details that matter: the Hiboost is listed for 4,000 sq ft, the ZORIDA for up to 2,000 sq ft with a 72dB gain, and the Phonetone and GAGBK for specific low bands used by Verizon and AT&T.

The honest reading of 5G on these listings is that the booster supports the 5G that carriers have deployed in large numbers on existing 4G bands, not every flavour of 5G. The Phonetone lists Band 12, 13 and 17, and the GAGBK lists Band 13 at 700MHz, which are the low bands that carry much of that traffic. A kit that does not list your carrier's bands cannot help, however many times it says 5G.
The usual rule applies: a booster amplifies an existing outdoor signal, so check the bars first.

products.name: HiBoost Home and Office Booster (4,000 sq ft)
products.description:
The Hiboost 4,000 sq ft kit is the broadest pick in this group, listed for homes, offices, shops and metal buildings with support for all U.S. and Canadian carriers. It states 5G compatibility, and it is a midpoint in size between the small ZORIDA and the larger kits found elsewhere. For a typical single-family home, that scale is about right.

The tradeoff is price, as it sits at the top of the roundup. The 5G claim is carefully worded in the listing, which refers to the 5G that is largely deployed rather than every type. As with any booster, real coverage depends on the outdoor signal.

Ownership is routine once the antennas are placed. Against the HiBoost 2,000 sq ft kit it doubles the listed area, and against the ZORIDA it lists no gain figure but covers all carriers. If you want a balanced 5G-ready kit for a house, it is the one.
pros: Supports all U.S. and Canadian carriers
Works for metal buildings and shops
cons: Top price tier among the five
No gain figure in the brief

products.name: HiBoost Home Office Booster (2,000 sq ft)
products.description:
The smaller HiBoost is for 2,000 sq ft and is listed for all service providers with 5G and 4G LTE compatibility. It promises lag-free signal and faster internet connections for a home office or small home. It supports several devices at once.

Its limit is simply size, since a house with several bedrooms will outgrow it. It also sits in a high price tier for such a small kit, and the brief gives no gain or band numbers. The 5G wording is again about compatibility, not a guarantee.

The install is standard and it asks little after setup. Against the ZORIDA it lists the same 2,000 sq ft but no gain figure, and it costs more. For a single room or small flat, it is a safe choice.

products.name: ZORIDA Booster with 72dB Gain
products.description:
The ZORIDA lists a 72dB gain, the highest figure in this roundup, with coverage up to 2,000 sq ft for several devices at once. It supports all U.S. carriers and 5G, and it can be used without registering with the carrier. That high gain suits a weak outdoor signal where more amplification is needed.

The tradeoff is that a high gain makes antenna separation more critical, because a close outside antenna can force the booster to cut power. The 2,000 sq ft coverage is also smaller than the Hiboost kit. It sits in the middle of the price range and is described as affordable and effective.

It asks for a bit more planning at install because of that gain. Against the Phonetone at 65dB it lists more gain but covers more carriers and a smaller area. For a small home with a weak signal, it is the strongest on paper.
products.bestFor: Small homes with a weak outdoor signal

products.name: Phonetone Booster for Band 12/13/17 (65dB)
products.description:
The Phonetone is aimed squarely at Verizon and AT&T, with Band 12, 13 and 17 and a listed 65dB gain. Automatic gain control detects the existing signal and adjusts, and the listing highlights VoLTE and 4G LTE data support alongside 5G. Focusing on these bands is exactly how most 5G coverage is actually delivered to existing phones.

The tradeoff is narrower carrier support, because T-Mobile subscribers on other bands will not benefit. The brief lists no coverage area, so you size it by gain and need. It sits in the middle of the price range.

Installation is the standard outside plus inside arrangement. Against the GAGBK it adds Band 12 and 17 alongside Band 13, so it covers AT&T too. For a Verizon or AT&T home, it is a sensible 5G-era pick.
cons: No coverage area in the brief

products.name: GAGBK Verizon Band 13 Booster
products.description:
The GAGBK is a Verizon kit that covers Band 13 on 700MHz and also works with Straight Talk. The listing claims excellent voice quality, fast 4G LTE and 5G data and support for multiple users. Because it targets one band, the match to a Verizon phone is clear.

That narrow focus is also its limit, as a household on other carriers gets nothing from it. The brief gives no gain or coverage figure, and the listing leans on marketing phrases. It sits in the lower price tier, which makes it an easy trial.

It is a standard antenna setup with little to maintain. Against the Phonetone it covers only Band 13, but costs less. For a Verizon family on a budget, it is a practical entry.
cons: No gain or coverage figures in the brief

buyingCriteria.explanation: Every kit here says 5G, but the listings tie that to the 5G carriers have deployed in large numbers on existing 4G bands. The Phonetone and GAGBK list low bands 12, 13 and 17 or 13 alone. A kit that does not list your carrier's bands will not help, so check the band list before the 5G label.

The ZORIDA lists 72dB, the Phonetone 65dB and the Hiboost no figure. Gain figures differ by source and are not a hard cap. A weak outdoor signal benefits from more gain, while a strong one cares more about output power.

Higher gain means higher feedback risk, so a 72dB unit like the ZORIDA needs more separation between antennas. Poor separation forces the booster to cut gain and, if that fails, shut off under FCC rules. Makers suggest roughly 25 to 30 feet vertically as a rule of thumb, while some models need more.

The GAGBK covers Verizon Band 13, the Phonetone covers 12, 13 and 17, and the Hiboost kits list all carriers. Look up your phone's bands before buying. Carrier band compatibility, coverage area and gain are the three variables to compare.
The Hiboost lists 4,000 sq ft, while the ZORIDA and smaller HiBoost list 2,000. These are best-case numbers, and no maker can guarantee them. Buy for the rooms that matter.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Look for approvals and a complete kit
buyingCriteria.explanation: Consumer boosters ship as kits with antennas and cables and should carry an FCC ID and network protection wording. The ZORIDA notes no carrier registration is needed, which fits that framework. Avoid listings that rely on marketing phrases and no real specs.

howWeEvaluated.title: 5G honesty
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at how each listing describes 5G support. The Hiboost wording ties it to 5G largely deployed, and the Phonetone lists real bands. Listings that rely only on the label scored lower.

howWeEvaluated.title: Gain and bands
howWeEvaluated.description: The ZORIDA leads on gain at 72dB, while the Phonetone gives bands 12, 13 and 17 with 65dB. The GAGBK lists a single band.

howWeEvaluated.title: Coverage realism
howWeEvaluated.description: The Hiboost 4,000 sq ft and the 2,000 sq ft kits are plain about size. Listings with no area figure, like the Phonetone and GAGBK, were harder to compare.

howWeEvaluated.title: Carrier flexibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked which carriers each kit covers. The two HiBoost kits and ZORIDA cover all carriers, while the GAGBK is Verizon-focused. Flexibility mattered for mixed households.

howWeEvaluated.title: Overall value
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the strongest pick, the Hiboost 4,000 sq ft, against the most basic, the GAGBK. Value meant real fit for the household. This guide is based on product specs and buyer feedback, not hands-on lab work.

howToChoose.subheading: For Streaming and Video Calls Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Support for the carrier's main data bands, automatic gain control and multi-device capability. Video calls need steady upload as well as download.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Phonetone lists VoLTE and LTE data with 65dB gain, and the Hiboost 4,000 sq ft handles several devices across a larger home.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You need coverage for a whole house on any carrier. The Hiboost 4,000 sq ft kit is built for that, and the smaller HiBoost adds a known brand.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Everyone is on Verizon or AT&T. The GAGBK and Phonetone cost less and target the right bands.

howToChoose.note: The 5G label is not a reason to pay more by itself.

faq.q: How do I choose a 5G booster?
faq.a: Match bands to your carrier first, then pick by size and gain. The Phonetone lists bands 12, 13 and 17, and the ZORIDA lists 72dB. The 5G label alone tells you little.
The GAGBK is the lowest cost, the Phonetone and ZORIDA sit in the middle, and the HiBoost kits are premium. Check current figures with the buttons and match the spend to your house.

faq.q: Will a booster make my 5G faster?
faq.a: It strengthens the carrier's existing signal where you already get some, which can improve speed and reliability. It does not add new network capacity. Listings tie 5G support to the 5G largely deployed on existing bands.

faq.q: Does 72dB mean the ZORIDA is best?
faq.a: Not automatically. Gain figures differ by source, and high gain needs more antenna separation. A 65dB Phonetone with the right bands may serve a Verizon home as well.

faq.q: Why does my booster cut power?
faq.a: The antennas may be too close, causing feedback. The booster lowers gain and may shut off. Move them apart, often 25 to 30 feet vertically or more depending on the model.

faq.q: Does one booster cover every carrier?
faq.a: The two HiBoost kits and ZORIDA list all carriers, while the GAGBK is aimed at Verizon and Straight Talk. Check the bands your phone uses.
